newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian longer dates in demand, short end spurned.
newsitem.headline: Belgian longer dates in demand, short end spurned.

text.p: Longer-dated Belgian paper held up well on Thursday, supported by continued buying interest on back of the view that EMU would go ahead as planned and European economies would continue to converge, dealers said.

OLO 12 (2012) and 23 (2015) were particularly well-bid, a trader said, while the area before 2002 was being sold on a mix of franc weakness, firming short rates amid tight liquidity and talk of Bundesbank action to defend a weaker mark.
"Flattening trades are still on the cards," one analyst said. Profit-taking in longer-dated paper would only create buying opportunities.
One analyst attacked the central bank's defence tactic for the franc, which has been under pressure with the mark.
"By tightening liquidity, confidence in the franc has evaporated -- repo players who had been buying Belgium are pulling out now that short rates are up and the cost of carry is up too," he said.

The selling, partly motivated by the franc's weakness, only undermined the franc further, he added. The National Bank should let rates fall, making Belgian paper interesting again and allowing the franc to recover to 20.63 to the mark. It was at 20.6490/05 at 1020 GMT, down from 20.6485/00 late on Wednesday.

The franc continued to suffer from a market appetite for hard non-EMU currencies, failing to draw much support from vague talk that the Bundesbank might set a variable rate repo tender at today's regular council meeting.
In such a tender rates would most likely rise, supporting the mark, and in turn the closely-linked franc.
Pressure has been building up on the mark amid a growing conviction that a broad-based, and consequently weakish, euro will be launched on time.
"The weakening mark has brought rate hikes closer, perhaps to the end of the year," one analyst said.
"The turnaround in Bundesbank policy may come sooner than expected," another said.

But a trader said he thought it unlikely the Bundesbank would raise rates before May of 1998, when the founding members of EMU are to be announced, since that might damage Germany's chances of being in the first wave of EMU entrants.

Market concern about a tightening, which would most likely be followed by Belgium, is reflected by Bibor futures BIB: where a spread of 20/30 basis points between September futures and March contracts has slipped to 10 bps, signalling a fall in expectations that rates will not go up before March.
Meanwhile, one-week repo rates continued to pound ahead, approaching the four percent mark, which is nearly a full point above the National Bank's 3.00 percent central rate.
One-week repos were at 3.90/95 percent, up from 3.85/90 earlier on Thursday and 3.65/70 late on Wednesday. Two months ago the rate was at around 3.25.
